where: Section 2, first paragraph ("A simple decoder is an AND gate..." )
problem: The gate described contradicts its stated output. An AND gate whose inputs are address lines (some inverted) goes HIGH exactly when the address pattern matches. That is an active-HIGH select, not active-low CS. Driving an active-low CS needs a NAND gate, or an AND gate followed by an inverter.
fix: A simple decoder is a NAND gate. Its inputs are the high address lines, some inverted. Its output is active-low CS: it goes to 0 only when the address matches the base pattern. An AND gate with an inverter on its output does the same job.

problem: "A19-A0 and BHE/A0 select banks" is compressed and a student can read it as if the whole address bus selects banks. It is BHE and A0 that choose the byte bank.
fix: In an 8086 system the memory is two byte banks. BHE low selects the high bank and A0 low selects the low bank. The decoder still compares the high address lines with the base address. A 2K chip still needs 11 address lines.

problem: "the memory-read control, RD when IO/M is low" is not a signal; RD alone is low for I/O reads too, so a student may wire RD straight to OE.
fix: Make a memory-read signal MEMR = RD OR IO/M. MEMR is low only when RD is low and IO/M is low. Connect MEMR to the ROM OE and the RAM OE. In the same way make MEMW = WR OR IO/M and connect it to the RAM WE.

problem: The setup is muddled. Partial decoding normally shows one chip at many ranges (mirroring); here two chips are both placed in the identical range, which is a wiring clash rather than a partial-decoding example.
fix: Two 2K chips are decoded with only A15 and A14; A13, A12 and A11 are left out. Explain that each chip then appears at several ranges and the two ranges overlap, so both chips can be selected together and fight on the data bus. A13 must be decoded to separate them.
